hints: First find the large arching vessel leaving the left ventricle in Fig. 6.1, then think about exactly where a valve must sit to stop blood falling back into the ventricle when it relaxes.
walkthrough:
Locate the Aorta and Left Ventricle**
You are looking at the left side of the heart where oxygenated blood is pumped out to the body. The aorta is the big arch at the top centre, labelled X, arising from the thick-walled left ventricle.

Place the Aortic Semilunar Valve**
Any vessel leaving a ventricle has a semilunar valve at its base to prevent backflow when ventricular pressure falls. The valve cusps at the base of the aorta are labelled S, sitting between the left ventricle and the aorta.

hints: Remember the rule that all veins carry blood toward the heart, but the pulmonary vein is unusual because it carries oxygenated blood away from the lungs.
Now look for the vessel entering the left atrium on the right side of Fig. 6.1 and match it to labels Q to X.
walkthrough:
Recall the Pulmonary Circulation**
Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and must return to the left atrium to be pumped to the body. The vessel doing this job is the pulmonary vein, even though most veins carry deoxygenated blood.

Read the Diagram**
On the right side of Fig. 6.1 you can see vessels entering the thin-walled left atrium. Label R points to one of these vessels coming from the lung direction, while Q is the aorta and W is the vena cava. So R is the pulmonary vein.
Final answer: name: pulmonary vein; label: R

hints: Think about where blood first enters the heart from the body and where an impulse needs to start so the wave of excitation can sweep across both atria from the top down.
walkthrough:
Think Like the Pacemaker**
The sinoatrial node sets the rhythm by generating a wave of excitation that makes the atria contract together. To do that it must sit in the atrial wall itself, where the muscle can pick up the signal immediately.

Pinpoint the Right Atrium**
Deoxygenated blood from the vena cava enters the right atrium first, so starting the beat there pushes blood in the correct direction. The node lies in the wall of the right atrium, near where the vena cava enters.
Final answer: in the wall (muscle) of the right atrium

hints: Start from what happens after the sinoatrial node fires - the atria contract, but the ventricles must not contract at the same moment, so trace where the excitation goes next.
Think about why a short pause before the signal passes down the septum would be useful for moving blood from atria into ventricles.
walkthrough:
Pass the Signal Onward**
After the sinoatrial node fires, excitation spreads over the atria and reaches the atrioventricular node between the atria and ventricles. The atrioventricular node picks up this wave and passes it to the bundle of His and then to the Purkyne fibres running down the septum to the base of the ventricles.

Create Time for Filling**
The atrioventricular node does not pass the impulse on instantly. It imposes a short delay of about 0.1 s. During this pause the atria finish contracting and empty blood into the ventricles, so the ventricles are fully filled before they contract from the apex upward. Without this, atria and ventricles would contract together and pumping would be inefficient.

Final answer: passes the wave of excitation to the Purkyne fibres down the septum; imposes a short delay so atria contract and empty fully and ventricles fill before ventricular contraction, preventing simultaneous contraction of atria and ventricles.
